name: Microservices

beginner.content:
What is a Microservice?

A microservice is a small, independently deployable service that implements a single business capability and communicates with other services over a network, typically via HTTP/REST or messaging. A microservices architecture is a style of building an application as a suite of such services, rather than one large deployable unit.

Where It Came From

• Early enterprise apps were built as monoliths - one codebase, one deployable artifact (a WAR/JAR), one database.
• SOA (Service-Oriented Architecture) in the 2000s introduced the idea of splitting a system into services, but usually with a heavyweight shared bus (ESB) and coarse-grained services.
• Microservices (the term popularized around 2011-2014, notably by companies like Netflix and Amazon) pushed this further - fine-grained services, each owning its own data, deployed and scaled independently, with lightweight communication (REST/messaging instead of a heavyweight ESB).

Key Characteristics

• Small and focused - each service does one thing (e.g. "Order Service", "Payment Service", "Inventory Service").
• Independently deployable - you can deploy a change to the Payment Service without redeploying the entire application.
• Owns its own data - each service typically has its own database; other services never reach directly into it.
• Organized around business capability - services are split by what the business does (orders, payments, shipping), not by technical layer (UI, logic, data).
• Communicates over the network - via REST, gRPC, or asynchronous messaging, since services run as separate processes (often on separate machines/containers).

expert.content:
The Honest Tradeoffs

Microservices are frequently sold as an unambiguous upgrade over monoliths - they aren't. They trade one set of problems for another.

What You Gain

• Independent deployability - ship a fix to one service without a full-system release.
• Independent scalability - scale only the service under load (e.g. Checkout during a sale), not the whole app.
• Team autonomy - different teams own different services, choose their own release cadence, even their own tech stack.
• Fault isolation - (if done right) one service crashing doesn't necessarily take down the whole system.

What It Costs You

• Operational complexity - you now have N deployables, N sets of logs, N things that can be down, instead of one.
• Network latency and failure modes - an in-process method call becomes a network call, which can be slow or simply fail (the network is not reliable).
• Distributed debugging - a single user request may touch 6 services; tracing what went wrong requires distributed tracing tooling, not just a stack trace.
• Data consistency challenges - no more simple cross-table SQL joins/transactions across services owning different data (see Distributed Data Management).
• Testing complexity - integration/end-to-end tests now need multiple services running together.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a microservice?A small, independently deployable service implementing one business capability, communicating with others over the network
How do microservices differ from SOA?SOA typically used a heavyweight shared ESB and coarser services; microservices favor fine-grained services with lightweight REST/messaging and no central bus
Name two real costs of microservices, not just benefitsOperational complexity (many deployables to run/monitor) and distributed debugging (a single request spans multiple services, requiring tracing tools)
Why do microservices typically own their own database?To keep each service independently deployable and loosely coupled - shared databases create hidden coupling between services

beginner.content:
Monolith vs Microservices

A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all of an application's functionality - one codebase, one build, one deployment, usually one database. A microservices architecture splits that same functionality across many independently deployable services.

Comparison

AspectMonolithMicroservices
Deployment unitOne (whole app deployed together)Many (each service deployed independently)
DatabaseUsually one shared databaseTypically one database per service
ScalingScale the entire app, even if only one part is under loadScale just the service under load
Team structureOne team (or many teams sharing one codebase)Small teams, each owning one or a few services
Technology choiceOne stack for the whole appEach service can use a different stack (polyglot)
Operational overheadLow - one thing to deploy/monitorHigh - many things to deploy/monitor/secure
Cross-feature transactionsSimple - one local DB transactionHard - needs patterns like Saga (see Microservices Design Patterns course)

expert.content:
"Monolith First" - The Migration Strategy

A well-known piece of advice (popularized by Martin Fowler) is: start with a monolith, and only split into microservices once you actually feel the pain that microservices solve.

Why Start With a Monolith

• Early on, the business domain isn't well understood yet - it's hard to draw good service boundaries before you know where they should be.
• A monolith is simpler to build, test, deploy, and debug - which matters most when a small team is moving fast and the product itself is still changing.
• Splitting too early, along the wrong boundaries, creates a "distributed monolith" - all the operational cost of microservices, none of the independence benefit, because services still have to change together.

When Microservices Start Paying Off

• The team has grown large enough that multiple teams stepping on each other's toes in one codebase is a real bottleneck.
• Specific parts of the system need very different scaling profiles (e.g. a recommendation engine needs way more compute than the user-profile service).
• Domain boundaries have become clear enough (often via Domain-Driven Design's "bounded contexts") to split along seams that will stay stable.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
When is a monolith the right choice?Small teams, early-stage products, or when domain boundaries aren't well understood yet - simplicity beats independence at that stage
What is a "distributed monolith"?A microservices split done along the wrong boundaries - services still have to change together, so you get microservices' operational cost without their independence benefit
What does "monolith first" advise?Start with a monolith and split into microservices only once you feel real pain (team scale, differing scaling needs) that justifies the added operational complexity

beginner.content:
What Makes a Service "Micro"

Not every small service is automatically well-designed - certain characteristics distinguish a well-built microservice from just "a small program that happens to run separately":

• Single Responsibility - a service should do one thing and do it well (one bounded business capability), not several unrelated things bundled together.
• Decentralized Data Management - each service owns its own database/schema; no other service reaches directly into it. Data is only accessed through the owning service's API.
• Independent Deployability - a service can be deployed on its own schedule, without coordinating a release with every other service.
• Technology Heterogeneity (Polyglot) - one service can be written in Java/Spring Boot, another in Node.js, another in Go - each team picks what fits their service best.
• Failure Isolation - one service failing shouldn't (ideally) cascade and take down every other service (this is why patterns like Circuit Breaker exist - see the Microservices Design Patterns course).
• Smart Endpoints, Dumb Pipes - business logic lives inside the services themselves; the communication mechanism between them (HTTP, a message broker) stays simple, not a heavyweight orchestration engine.

expert.content:
Sizing a Service - "Micro" Doesn't Mean "Tiny"

A common beginner misconception is that "microservice" means "as small as possible" (e.g. one service per database table). In practice, the right size is driven by bounded context (a Domain-Driven Design concept) - a service should be exactly as big as one coherent business capability, no bigger and no smaller.

Splitting too finely creates "nanoservices" - services so small that most requests still need to call 5+ other services, multiplying the network-latency and failure-mode costs described in the Introduction topic, without a matching benefit.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does "decentralized data management" mean?Each service owns its own database; other services can only reach that data through the owning service's API, never directly
What does "smart endpoints, dumb pipes" mean?Business logic lives in the services themselves; the communication layer (HTTP/message broker) stays simple rather than embedding orchestration logic
Why is "as small as possible" the wrong sizing goal?Splitting too finely creates "nanoservices" where most requests fan out across many services, multiplying network/failure costs without a matching benefit - size should follow bounded context, not an arbitrary smallness target

beginner.content:
How Services Talk to Each Other

Since each microservice runs as a separate process, they must communicate over the network. There are two broad styles:

• Synchronous - the caller sends a request and waits/blocks for a response (REST over HTTP, or gRPC for a faster, typed, binary protocol).
• Asynchronous - the caller sends a message/event and moves on without waiting for an immediate response (via a message broker - see the Integration & Messaging Patterns course for the full catalog).

expert.content:
Choosing Between Styles

AspectSynchronous (REST/gRPC)Asynchronous (Messaging)
CouplingTighter - caller needs the callee to be up and responsive right nowLooser - producer doesn't need consumer to be available at the same instant
LatencyCaller waits for the full round tripCaller can continue immediately (fire-and-forget or eventual reply)
ResilienceA slow/down callee directly stalls/fails the caller (needs Circuit Breaker/Timeout)A down consumer just means messages queue up until it recovers
Best forRequests that genuinely need an immediate answer (e.g. "is this in stock right now?")Workflows that can tolerate eventual processing (e.g. "send a confirmation email")

gRPC vs REST: gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers (binary, strongly typed, code-generated clients/servers), which is typically faster and more bandwidth-efficient than JSON-over-REST, at the cost of being less human-readable/debuggable and less universally supported by simple tools like curl/browsers.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the key tradeoff between sync and async communication?Sync is simpler to reason about but couples the caller to the callee's availability/latency right now; async is more resilient/decoupled but adds eventual-consistency complexity
Why might gRPC be chosen over REST between internal services?Faster/more compact binary serialization (Protocol Buffers) and strongly-typed generated clients, at the cost of human-readability and universal tool support

beginner.content:
Why You Can't Just Hardcode a URL

In a microservices system running on containers/cloud infrastructure, service instances come and go - they scale up/down, restart, and get new IP addresses constantly. Hardcoding http://192.168.1.5:8081 for the Order Service simply breaks the moment that instance restarts elsewhere.

The Fix: Service Registry and Discovery

• A service registry is a directory where every service instance registers itself on startup ("I am Order Service, running at this address") and deregisters on shutdown.
• Service discovery is how a caller finds a live instance of the service it needs, by asking the registry instead of using a hardcoded address.
• Client-side discovery - the calling service queries the registry itself and picks an instance (possible load-balancing client-side).
• Server-side discovery - the caller talks to a load balancer/router, which queries the registry on the caller's behalf.

expert.content:
Netflix Eureka - A Concrete Example

Spring Cloud Netflix Eureka is a widely-used service registry in the Spring ecosystem.
codeExamples:
# Eureka Server - application.yml
server:
  port: 8761
eureka:
  client:
    register-with-eureka: false
    fetch-registry: false

# Order Service (a Eureka Client) - application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
eureka:
  client:
    service-url:
      defaultZone: http://localhost:8761/eureka/

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is hardcoding service URLs a problem in microservices?Instances scale/restart/move constantly in containerized environments, so a fixed IP:port breaks as soon as the instance changes
Client-side vs server-side discovery?Client-side: the caller queries the registry itself and picks an instance. Server-side: the caller talks to a load balancer that queries the registry on its behalf
What does Eureka provide in the Spring ecosystem?A service registry that services register with on startup and query to find live instances of other services by logical name

For a deeper dive specifically framed as a design pattern (including client-side vs server-side tradeoffs in more depth), see "Service Discovery Pattern" in the Microservices Design Patterns course.

beginner.content:
Combining Data From Multiple Services

A single screen in a client app (e.g. an order-detail page) often needs data that lives across several services - order details from Order Service, item info from Catalog Service, shipping status from Shipping Service. API Composition is the practice of combining results from multiple service calls into one response for the client.

Two Ways to Compose

• Client-side composition - the client itself calls each service separately and merges the results (simple, but chatty over the network and exposes internal service boundaries to the client).
• API Gateway-side composition - a single gateway/aggregator service calls all the needed backend services and returns one combined response to the client (client makes just one call; see the "API Gateway Pattern" and "Aggregator Pattern" in the Microservices Design Patterns course for the deeper pattern treatment).

expert.content:
The N+1 Problem Across Services

A subtle trap: composing a list of items where each item then requires its OWN follow-up call to another service (e.g. fetch 20 orders, then call Catalog Service once PER order to get item names) results in 1 + 20 = 21 network calls instead of 2. This "N+1" problem, familiar from ORMs, is even more expensive across a network than within a single database.

Mitigations

• Batch endpoints - ask the Catalog Service for many item IDs in one call instead of one call per item.
• Caching frequently-composed, slow-changing data.
• Denormalizing some data into the composing service if the read pattern justifies it (accepting some duplication for read performance).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is API composition?Combining results from multiple backend service calls into one response for the client
Client-side vs gateway-side composition?Client-side: the client itself calls each service and merges results. Gateway-side: one gateway/aggregator does the calling and merging, client makes one call
What is the N+1 problem in a microservices context?Composing a list where each item requires its own follow-up service call, multiplying network calls (1 list call + N per-item calls) - fixed by batch endpoints or caching

beginner.content:
Why Containers Matter for Microservices

With dozens of independently deployable services, each potentially needing a different runtime/dependency version, running them all directly on a shared host becomes unmanageable ("works on my machine" multiplied by N services). Containers solve this by packaging a service together with everything it needs (JVM, libraries, config) into one portable, isolated unit.

What Docker Gives You

• Consistent runtime - the exact same container image runs identically on a developer's laptop, in CI, and in production.
• Isolation - each container has its own filesystem/process space, so services don't fight over dependency versions.
• Fast startup - containers start in seconds, much faster than provisioning a full VM, which matters for scaling up quickly under load.
A Minimal Dockerfile for a Spring Boot Service
codeExamples:
# Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/order-service-0.0.1.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8081
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Build and run
docker build -t order-service:1.0 .
docker run -p 8081:8081 order-service:1.0

# The service is now reachable at http://localhost:8081

expert.content:
Multi-Service Local Development with Docker Compose

Running several services (and their dependencies like a database) by hand quickly becomes tedious. Docker Compose lets you define and start a whole multi-container setup with one command.
codeExamples:
# docker-compose.yml
version: "3.8"
services:
  order-service:
    build: ./order-service
    ports:
      - "8081:8081"
    depends_on:
      - order-db

  order-db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: orders
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

  inventory-service:
    build: ./inventory-service
    ports:
      - "8083:8083"

# Start everything defined above
docker compose up

# Illustrative: requires the referenced service directories/Dockerfiles
# to exist; shown to demonstrate multi-service local orchestration,
# not as a standalone runnable snippet.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why are containers a natural fit for microservices?They package each service with its exact runtime/dependencies into a portable, isolated unit that runs identically everywhere and starts in seconds
What problem does Docker Compose solve?Defining and starting a whole multi-service (+ dependencies like a DB) local setup with one command, instead of manually running each container
What's the difference between a Docker image and a container?An image is the packaged, immutable blueprint (filesystem + config); a container is a running instance of that image

beginner.content:
Why Do You Need an Orchestrator Beyond Plain Docker?

Docker packages and runs a single container, but running dozens of microservices in production raises questions Docker alone doesn't answer:

• Scaling - if traffic spikes, who starts more container instances?
• Self-healing - if a container crashes, who restarts it?
• Rolling updates - how do you deploy a new version with zero downtime?
• Service networking - how do containers on different hosts find each other?

Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestration platform that answers all of these - it schedules containers across a cluster of machines, restarts failed ones, scales them up/down, and load-balances traffic between them.

Core Kubernetes Concepts

ConceptWhat It Is
PodThe smallest deployable unit - one or more tightly-coupled containers sharing network/storage
DeploymentManages a set of identical Pod replicas, handles rolling updates and self-healing
ServiceA stable network endpoint (IP/DNS name) that load-balances traffic across a Deployment's Pods, even as Pods come and go
NamespaceA virtual cluster-within-a-cluster, used to separate environments/teams (e.g. dev, staging, prod)

Pods are ephemeral - they can be killed and recreated with a new IP address at any time. This is exactly why a stable Service abstraction sits in front of them.

A Minimal Deployment + Service for a Spring Boot App

This YAML manifest runs 3 replicas of a Spring Boot microservice and exposes them through a stable Service:
codeExamples:
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: myregistry/order-service:1.0.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
---
# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: order-service
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP
# NOTE: illustrative Kubernetes manifest, not a runnable Java program

beginner.content:
Basic kubectl Commands

kubectl is the CLI used to interact with a Kubernetes cluster:
codeExamples:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml       # create/update resources from a manifest
kubectl get pods                       # list running pods
kubectl get deployments
kubectl scale deployment order-service --replicas=5   # manually scale
kubectl logs <pod-name>                # view a pod's logs
kubectl delete pod <pod-name>          # delete a pod (Deployment recreates it automatically)
# NOTE: shell commands, not Java - illustrative, no fabricated program output

expert.content:
How Kubernetes Achieves Self-Healing and Zero-Downtime Deploys

• A Deployment's controller loop constantly compares the desired replica count against the actual running Pods, and creates/deletes Pods to reconcile any difference - this is what makes a crashed Pod get automatically replaced.
• A rolling update replaces old Pods with new ones a few at a time (controlled by maxSurge/maxUnavailable), never taking all replicas down at once - this is how zero-downtime deploys work under the hood.
• Readiness probes tell Kubernetes when a Pod is actually ready to receive traffic (not just "started") - Spring Boot Actuator's /actuator/health/readiness endpoint is the standard hook for this.
• Liveness probes tell Kubernetes when a Pod is unhealthy and should be killed/restarted - distinct from readiness, since a Pod can be "alive" but temporarily not ready (e.g. still warming up a cache).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the difference between a Pod and a Deployment?A Pod is a single running instance of one or more containers; a Deployment manages a desired number of identical Pod replicas and handles their lifecycle (scaling, updates, healing)
Why does a Service exist if Pods already have IPs?Pod IPs change every time a Pod is recreated; a Service provides a stable, unchanging address that always routes to whichever Pods are currently healthy
Liveness probe vs readiness probe?Liveness answers "should this Pod be restarted?"; readiness answers "should this Pod currently receive traffic?" - a Pod can be alive but not ready

beginner.content:
The Database-Per-Service Principle

In a microservices architecture, each service owns its own database, and no other service is allowed to access it directly - all access goes through that service's API.

Order Service --owns--> Order DB
Inventory Service --owns--> Inventory DB
Payment Service --owns--> Payment DB

Order Service does NOT query Inventory DB directly.
It calls the Inventory Service's API instead.

If services shared one database, changing a table's schema in one service could silently break every other service reading from it - this defeats the entire point of independent deployability.

The Challenges This Creates

• No cross-service SQL joins - you can't JOIN orders WITH inventory across two databases, so a request needing combined data must call multiple services and merge the results in application code (see the API Composition topic).
• Eventual consistency - since each service commits to its own database independently, there's no single ACID transaction spanning services; data becomes consistent across services after some delay, not instantly.
• Distributed transactions - a business operation like "place an order" might need to update Order, Inventory, and Payment data together; a classic two-phase-commit transaction across databases doesn't scale well in this world.

expert.content:
How This Is Actually Solved in Practice

The standard solutions to distributed data challenges are covered in full depth in the Microservices Design Patterns course - this topic gives the conceptual framing, not the implementation detail:

• Saga Pattern - coordinating a multi-service transaction as a sequence of local transactions with compensating rollback actions on failure.
• CQRS - separating the read model from the write model, often letting reads be served from a denormalized view built specifically to avoid needing cross-service joins.
• Event Sourcing - storing state as an event log, which naturally supports building multiple read-optimized views across service boundaries.

The mental shift required: distributed systems trade the comfortable guarantees of a single ACID database for independent scalability and deployability - accepting eventual consistency is usually the price paid.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why can't two microservices share one database?Sharing a database recreates tight coupling through the schema - any change to a shared table risks breaking every service that reads it, defeating independent deployability
How do you query data that spans two services?Call each owning service's API and combine the results in application code (API Composition), or maintain a denormalized read view built for that purpose (CQRS)
What does "eventual consistency" mean here?Data across services becomes consistent after some propagation delay, rather than instantly within one atomic transaction, since each service commits independently to its own database

beginner.content:
Two Different Trust Boundaries to Secure

Microservices security has two distinct concerns:

• Client → API Gateway - authenticating and authorizing an external user/client hitting your system's public entry point.
• Service → Service - authenticating calls between your own internal services, so a compromised or rogue service can't freely call every other service.

   External Client
         |
     [OAuth2 / JWT]
         v
    API Gateway  ---centralized auth check happens here---
         |
     [mTLS / internal token]
         v
   Order Service --calls--> Inventory Service

OAuth2 and JWT for Client Authentication

• A client authenticates once (e.g. via username/password or an identity provider) and receives a JWT (JSON Web Token) - a signed, self-contained token carrying claims about who the user is and what they're allowed to do.
• The client sends this JWT on every subsequent request (typically in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header).
• Because the JWT is signed, any service can verify it's genuine without calling back to a central auth server on every request - it just checks the signature.

The API Gateway as the Natural Auth Chokepoint

Rather than every single microservice re-implementing token validation, it's common to validate authentication once at the API Gateway and pass a trusted identity downstream (e.g. as a header), keeping individual services simpler. This is a direct extension of the API Gateway pattern already covered in the Microservices Design Patterns course.

expert.content:
Securing Service-to-Service Calls: mTLS and Service Mesh

Client-facing auth (OAuth2/JWT) doesn't automatically secure the internal network between your own services - if an attacker gets inside the cluster network, unencrypted/unauthenticated service-to-service calls are wide open.

• mTLS (mutual TLS) - both sides of a service-to-service call present a certificate, so each service can cryptographically verify who's actually calling it, not just encrypt the traffic.
• Rolling out mTLS by hand across every service is painful - this is one of the main reasons a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) exists: it injects a sidecar proxy next to every service that handles mTLS transparently, without changing application code.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is a signed JWT useful for microservices?Any service can verify it independently by checking the signature, without a round-trip call to a central auth server on every request
Why isn't client authentication enough to secure a microservices system?It only secures the boundary between the external client and the API Gateway; internal service-to-service calls need their own trust mechanism (e.g. mTLS)
What problem does a service mesh solve for security?It transparently provides mTLS and identity between services via sidecar proxies, without requiring every service to implement that logic itself

beginner.content:
The Testing Pyramid, Adapted for Microservices

          /\
         /E2E\        <- few, slow, brittle, expensive
        /------\
       /Contract\      <- verify services agree without full deployment
      /----------\
     /Integration \    <- test a service against real dependencies (DB, etc.)
    /--------------\
   /   Unit Tests   \  <- many, fast, cheap, test logic in isolation
  /------------------\
The shape stays the same as traditional testing (lots of fast unit tests, fewer slow end-to-end tests), but microservices add a layer traditional monoliths don't need: contract testing.

Unit and Integration Tests

• Unit tests - test a single class/method's logic in isolation, mocking out dependencies. Fast, run on every commit.
• Integration tests - test a service against its real dependencies (an actual test database, e.g. via Testcontainers), verifying the service's own code + its direct infrastructure work together correctly.

Why Full End-to-End Tests Don't Scale Well

An end-to-end test that spins up every microservice in the system to verify one user flow is: slow (many services to boot), brittle (any one service being flaky fails the whole test), and hard to debug (a failure could be in any of a dozen services). The practical answer is to minimize how many of these you rely on and lean on contract testing instead for verifying inter-service compatibility.

expert.content:
Contract Testing

Contract testing (e.g. using the Pact framework) verifies that a service ("consumer") and the service it calls ("provider") agree on the shape of their API contract - without actually running both services together.

The flow: the consumer team writes a test defining what it expects from the provider's response; this generates a "contract" file; the provider team then runs that contract against their own service in CI to verify they still satisfy it. If the provider changes its API in a breaking way, the contract test fails in the provider's own pipeline - long before a real integration bug reaches production.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why are full end-to-end tests risky to rely on heavily in microservices?They're slow to run, brittle (any dependent service's flakiness fails the test), and hard to debug since a failure could originate in any of many services
What does contract testing verify that integration testing doesn't?That two independently-deployed services still agree on their API contract, without needing to actually run both together
Where does a Pact-style contract test run?The consumer generates the contract; the provider replays and verifies it against their own service independently in their own CI pipeline

beginner.content:
Rolling Deployment

Replaces old-version instances with new-version instances gradually, a few at a time, so the service never has zero running instances.

[v1][v1][v1][v1]   start: 4 old instances
[v2][v1][v1][v1]   replace one at a time...
[v2][v2][v1][v1]
[v2][v2][v2][v1]
[v2][v2][v2][v2]   done: all new
This is Kubernetes' default Deployment update strategy. Low infrastructure cost, but if v2 has a bug, some real users hit it before you notice and roll back.

Blue-Green Deployment

Run two complete environments - "blue" (current live version) and "green" (new version) - side by side. Once green is fully tested, switch all traffic to it at once (usually by repointing a load balancer/router).

• Rollback is instant - just switch traffic back to blue.
• Costs roughly 2x the infrastructure while both environments exist.

Canary Deployment

Route a small percentage of real traffic (e.g. 5%) to the new version while the rest keeps hitting the old version, then gradually increase the percentage as confidence grows.

• Limits the "blast radius" of a bad release to a small fraction of users.
• Requires good monitoring to actually detect problems in that 5% before rolling further.

expert.content:
Comparing the Three Strategies

StrategyDowntime RiskInfra CostRollback SpeedK8s Primitive
RollingLowLow (no duplicate env)Slow (roll forward/back gradually)Deployment (default strategy)
Blue-GreenVery lowHigh (2x during switch)Instant (repoint traffic)Two Deployments + Service switch
CanaryVery lowModerateFast (shift traffic weight back)Service mesh traffic splitting, or Ingress weight rules

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the main tradeoff of blue-green deployment?Very fast, safe rollback since it's just a traffic switch, but at the cost of running two full environments simultaneously
Why is canary deployment considered lower-risk than rolling?It exposes the new version to only a small, controlled percentage of real traffic first, limiting how many users are affected if there's a problem, before rolling out further

beginner.content:
What Is the Twelve-Factor App?

The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology (originating from Heroku) describing best practices for building software-as-a-service applications that are portable, scalable, and suited to modern cloud/container deployment - it's a foundational influence on how cloud-native and microservices applications are designed today.

The 12 Factors, Briefly

#FactorIdea
1CodebaseOne codebase tracked in version control, many deploys
2DependenciesExplicitly declare and isolate dependencies (no relying on system-wide packages)
3ConfigStore config in the environment, not in code
4Backing ServicesTreat databases/queues/etc. as attached resources, swappable via config
5Build, Release, RunStrictly separate the build, release, and run stages
6ProcessesExecute the app as one or more stateless processes
7Port BindingExport services via port binding, not relying on a runtime-injected web server
8ConcurrencyScale out via the process model (run more instances), not by making one process bigger
9DisposabilityFast startup and graceful shutdown maximize robustness
10Dev/Prod ParityKeep development, staging, and production as similar as possible
11LogsTreat logs as event streams, don't manage log files yourself
12Admin ProcessesRun admin/management tasks as one-off processes in the same environment

expert.content:
Why This Methodology Underpins Cloud-Native Design

• Factor 3 (Config) is exactly the Externalized Configuration Pattern covered in the Cloud-Native Patterns course - Spring Boot's application.yml + environment-variable overrides is a direct, practical implementation of this factor.
• Factor 6 (stateless processes) is precisely why Kubernetes can freely kill and recreate Pods without losing anything important - state belongs in a backing service (a database), never in the process's own memory.
• Factor 9 (disposability) directly maps to Kubernetes' readiness/liveness probes and rolling deployments - a service that can't start/stop quickly and cleanly breaks orchestration.
• Factor 11 (logs as event streams) is the reasoning behind centralized logging (ELK/EFK) rather than services managing their own log files on disk, which vanish the moment a container is destroyed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why does the Twelve-Factor App insist on statelessness?Stateless processes can be freely killed, restarted, and scaled by an orchestrator without any risk of losing data, since all real state lives in a backing service
How does Factor 3 (Config) relate to a container image?The same built container image should be deployable to dev/staging/prod unchanged - only its externally-injected configuration differs between environments

beginner.content:
Why Observability Matters More in Microservices

In a monolith, a slow request means looking in one place - the monolith's own logs and stack traces. In a microservices system, a single user request might pass through a dozen services before returning a response - if it's slow or fails, which service is actually responsible?

Client -> API Gateway -> Order Service -> Inventory Service -> Payment Service -> ...
                                              ^
                              which one is actually slow? without observability, you're guessing.

The Three Pillars of Observability

PillarAnswersExample Tooling
LogsWhat exactly happened, in detail, at a point in time?ELK/EFK stack
MetricsHow is the system behaving in aggregate, over time? (latency, error rate, throughput)Prometheus + Grafana
TracesWhat path did one specific request take across services, and where did time go?Spring Cloud Sleuth, Zipkin, Jaeger

These three pillars are covered in much greater practical depth as Centralized Logging and Distributed Tracing in the Cloud-Native Patterns course - this topic exists to tie them together conceptually as one overall observability strategy, not to duplicate that depth.

expert.content:
Logs, Metrics, and Traces Are Complementary, Not Redundant

A typical debugging flow uses all three together: a metric dashboard shows latency spiked at 2:15pm → a trace for a slow request in that window shows most of the time was spent in the Inventory Service call → the Inventory Service's logs at that exact timestamp reveal it was retrying a failed database connection.

None of the three alone tells the full story - metrics tell you something is wrong and roughly when, traces tell you where in the call chain, and logs tell you why.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is observability a bigger deal for microservices than monoliths?A single request in a monolith stays in one process, but in microservices it crosses many services - you need dedicated tooling (traces) just to see the path a request took
What's the difference between a metric and a trace?A metric is an aggregate number over time (e.g. average latency across all requests); a trace follows one specific request's journey across every service it touched

cheatNotes: Microservice = small, independently deployable service owning one business capability
Monolith first - split into microservices only once you feel real pain that justifies it
Each microservice should own its own database - no other service reaches into it directly
Synchronous (REST/gRPC) = simpler but tightly coupled; Asynchronous (messaging) = resilient but eventually consistent
Service registry + discovery replaces hardcoded URLs since instances scale/restart constantly
API composition combines multiple services' data into one client-facing response - watch for the N+1 problem
Docker packages a service + its runtime into one portable, isolated, fast-starting unit
Docker Compose orchestrates multiple local containers (services + DB) with one command
